fields.platform: Platform name as shown on the site.
fields.country: Territory name as recorded — may be a state or disputed territory; see iso and subnational.
fields.iso: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code of the (parent) country.
fields.subnational: True when the row is a state-level or territorial measure, not a national one.
fields.since: Free-text date the restriction started or takes effect.
fields.notes: Case-file text, when the row has something platform-specific to say.
fields.source: Cited URL. Empty for default-restricted countries with no platform-specific reporting (see the site's methodology).

entries.notes: Blocked in May 2017 during the Gulf diplomatic rift. Despite the 2021 Al-Ula Declaration restoring regional diplomatic ties, digital access to Al Jazeera remains restricted.
Blocked in May 2017 alongside dozens of news outlets, following earlier broadcast bans.
In May 2024, Israel passed emergency legislation permitting the government to shut down Al Jazeera's local offices, confiscate equipment, and block access to its broadcasts and websites.

Al Jazeera's English-language website became unreachable from Pakistani networks on 3 August 2026, a day after the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting accused the broadcaster of "yellow journalism" over its coverage of the Azad Jammu and Kashmir elections. JournalismPakistan verified that the site could not be reached over multiple Pakistani connections and browsers. Neither the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority nor the ministry has acknowledged ordering a block, and the Arabic service and television broadcasts are not reported as affected.

Access to Al Jazeera's websites was blocked and its operating licence revoked in May 2017. Despite the 2021 Al-Ula agreement restoring diplomatic relations, digital and broadcast restrictions in the Kingdom remain largely in place.

Blocked in May 2017 during the Gulf diplomatic dispute. Freedom House (Freedom on the Net 2024) and regional media monitoring confirm that the United Arab Emirates unblocked Al Jazeera's main websites (aljazeera.com and aljazeera.net) in early 2023 following post-Al-Ula normalization, though television broadcast licensing and local bureau operations remain subject to state regulation.
The government blocks almost all independent and foreign news sites in one of the worlds most censored media environments.
Islamic Republic of Iran maintains a highly restrictive internet censorship regime, frequently blocking access to foreign news outlets.

BBC Persian and the main BBC site are routinely blocked in Islamic Republic of Iran.
Access to the BBC News website was blocked following the invasion of Ukraine as part of a broader crackdown on foreign media.
The Vietnamese government has historically implemented blocks on the BBC’s websites (particularly its Vietnamese-language service).

Mississippi's HB 1126 requires social platforms to age-verify every user and obtain parental consent for minors. Bluesky pulled out of Mississippi entirely on 22 August 2025 rather than comply, then returned on 8 December 2025 as an 18+-only service in the state — adults must pass an age check and under-18s remain barred. Larger platforms had not implemented the checks while a Fifth Circuit appeal (NetChoice v. Fitch) remains pending.

Ofcom revoked CGTN's United Kingdom broadcast licence on 4 February 2021, finding that licence-holder Star China Media had no editorial responsibility for the channel's output, and it refused to transfer the licence to China Global Television Network Corporation because that body is ultimately controlled by the Chinese Communist Party — which United Kingdom broadcasting law does not permit.

CGTN was compelled to register under the Foreign Agents Registration Act in February 2019 and had its congressional press passes revoked. In February 2020 the State Department designated it one of five Chinese state media entities treated as foreign missions — a status normally reserved for embassies and consulates — requiring it to report staff names, turnover and property holdings to the Office of Foreign Missions. The designation carries no restriction on what CGTN may publish.
Blocked by the Great Firewall. Domestic AI alternatives are heavily promoted and regulated.
OpenAI blocks access to users in Cuba to comply with US sanctions.
Blocked by the government.
Briefly blocked by the Italian data protection authority (Garante) over GDPR concerns, but reinstated in April 2023 after compliance changes.
Blocked by the government.
OpenAI blocks access to users in Syria to comply with US sanctions.

Brazil's Digital Statute of Children and Adolescents (ECA Digital, Law 15,211/2025) took effect on 17 March 2026. Social media accounts for users under 16 must be linked to a legal guardian, and platforms must use reliable age verification — self-declaration alone is not allowed.

Brazil's National Data Protection Authority (ANPD) ordered Discord on 12 August 2026 to suspend its live video features within three business days, after an investigation prompted by the death of a 13-year-old girl during an online broadcast. Discord complied on 17 August 2026, switching off Go Live screen sharing and camera video inside servers and calls; text chat and voice calls remain available. The suspension stands until ANPD accepts the platform's child-safety safeguards — Discord has asked the agency to withdraw the order.

Discord access in Egypt appears intermittent: users and network measurements recorded a nationwide disruption on 11-12 January 2026 across major ISPs (including WE and Vodafone), where both discord.com and gateway.discord.gg stalled during TLS setup — indicating targeted filtering; service later resumed.

Gabon's Ordinance No. 0011/PR/2026 (signed 26 February 2026; published 8 April 2026) sets a digital age of majority of 16 and requires parental consent for under-16 social media access. Platforms must verify users with more than an age or ID check alone — name, address and Personal Identification Number (NIP) — ending online anonymity. Operators have a 12-month transition period, with full compliance expected by February 2027.
Blocked by government firewalls, particularly affecting voice and video calls.
Roskomnadzor blocked Discord in October 2024, citing violations of Russian law.

An Ankara court blocked Discord in October 2024 over child-safety concerns. As of June 2026 it remains blocked — ministers say Discord has met compliance criteria, but a fresh court ruling is required to restore access.
Discord's voice and video features are blocked by major United Arab Emirates ISPs under rules against unlicensed VoIP services; text chat generally works.

Discord rolled out United Kingdom age checks (face scan or ID) for sensitive content under the Online Safety Act in July 2025; a later breach at a third-party verification vendor exposed ID photos of about 70,000 users.

Blocked by the Great Firewall since early September 2014, and still unreachable from the mainland. The authorities have never said why it was blocked. It remains accessible from the special administrative regions of Hong Kong and Macau, which sit outside the Great Firewall.

Indonesia blocked DuckDuckGo in July 2024; the communications ministry later confirmed the ban, citing complaints that its search results facilitated access to online gambling and pornography, which are illegal in the country.
Access is frequently restricted or blocked due to Islamic Republic of Iran's systemic censorship infrastructure.
The Taliban blocked Deutsche Welle broadcasts in Pashto and Dari in March 2022 alongside other foreign broadcasters.
Access to the Deutsche Welle website was blocked by Belarusian authorities in October 2021 as part of a crackdown on independent online news outlets.
In February 2022, Russia banned Deutsche Welle broadcasts and closed its Moscow bureau, and subsequently blocked the dw.com website.
Türkiye's media regulator RTÜK blocked access to dw.com in June 2022 after Deutsche Welle declined to apply for a domestic online broadcast licence.
The Venezuelan government ordered DW Spanish removed from cable distribution in March 2024 and restricted website access following a report on state corruption.

Indonesia began deactivating under-16 accounts on designated high-risk platforms from 28 March 2026. The communications ministry named YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, Threads, X, Bigo Live and Roblox among platforms subject to the under-16 restriction.
Facebook has been banned since the 2009 Presidential elections and the subsequent protests.
Malaysia's under-16 social media ban took effect on 1 June 2026. Platforms must verify users' ages and remove under-16 accounts or face fines of up to RM1 million.
Facebook has been banned since the 2021 Military takeover.
Facebook has been banned since the Russian Invasion of Ukraine. The Russian government has restricted or banned social media platforms since then.

Türkiye's parliament passed a law in April 2026 banning social media services for children under 15 and requiring platforms to implement age-verification systems and parental control tools for older minors. The law takes effect six months after publication in the Official Gazette, with full compliance expected in late 2026. A separate e-government (e-Devlet) real-ID login scheme for all users was still a draft as of April 2026.

United Arab Emirates Cabinet resolution (announced 18 June 2026) bars children under 15 from creating, using or operating personal social media accounts. Platforms must use robust age-verification — including digital identity and AI-supported checks; self-declaration alone is not accepted — with enhanced safeguards for users aged 15 to under 16. Phase one covers X, Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok. Platforms have a 12-month transition, with full compliance expected by June 2027.

Blocked in People's Republic of China since July 2014 following a government crackdown on instant messaging apps, citing terrorism concerns. The Citizen Lab reported that the block was primarily implemented via DNS tampering and HTTP request filtering.

KakaoTalk is inaccessible due to Islamic Republic of Iran's broad internet censorship policies that block many foreign messaging platforms and cause SMS verification issues for users within the country.
Like most foreign messaging apps, KakaoTalk is blocked under Turkmenistan's severe state-controlled internet censorship.
KakaoTalk's VoIP features (voice and video calls) are strictly blocked by the Telecommunications and Digital Government Regulatory Authority (TDRA), which restricts unlicensed VoIP services.

Citizen Lab measured Great Firewall DNS tampering and HTTP filtering of LINE domains from mainland People's Republic of China, disrupting chat, contact, account and in-app-store functions. LINE said its messaging service was inaccessible in mainland People's Republic of China; current access requires a circumvention route.
Blocked by the Iranian judiciary alongside other messaging apps.
Oman maintains strict regulations on VoIP services, leading to blocks on apps like LINE to protect traditional telecommunications markets.
VoIP services, including those provided by third-party apps like LINE, have been subject to regulations that often limit or block their use in favor of state-licensed operators.

Roskomnadzor added LINE's chat servers to its banned-site register after the operator failed to register as an information-distribution service under Russian law, preventing users from sending and receiving messages.
LINE has faced bans and suspensions for failing to comply with local telecommunications regulations, restricting the app's VoIP calling functionalities.
Turkmenistan's state-controlled internet blocks foreign messaging services. Reporting has specifically identified LINE among the blocked mobile messengers.
United Arab Emirates telecom controls throttle LINE's VoIP and communications functions as part of the licensing regime for foreign internet calling services; text messaging may remain available.
Restricted access due to US sanctions, resulting in account limitations for users in Islamic Republic of Iran, alongside government censorship.

Roskomnadzor blocked LinkedIn in November 2016 after a Moscow court ruled it violated a 2015 data-storage law requiring personal data of Russian citizens to be stored on servers located within the country.

Netflix has never been available in Crimea. When it expanded nearly worldwide in January 2016, Crimea was excluded alongside Syria, North Korea, and People's Republic of China due to U.S. government trade sanctions prohibiting U.S. companies from providing services to the region.
Netflix is unavailable in Islamic Republic of Iran due to US sanctions, and the service is also blocked by Iranian authorities.

Netflix suspended its service in Russia in March 2022 after the invasion of Ukraine, citing conditions on the ground, rising sanctions, and payment challenges. It had already paused future Russian projects and refused to carry state propaganda channels required under new Russian media rules.

Netflix has never offered service in Syria. When it expanded nearly worldwide in January 2016, Syria was excluded along with other territories subject to U.S. sanctions. The company still lists Syria among countries where Netflix is not available — a sanctions-driven restriction rather than a Syrian government block of the platform.

The Chinese government blocked the NYT website following an investigative report into the wealth of the family of then-Premier Wen Jiabao. Later, in 2016, Apple removed the NYT news apps from its People's Republic of China App Store for "violation of local regulations."

Saudi Arabia intermittently throttles or blocks access to the website and specific critical articles during politically sensitive times, such as the period following the 2018 murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi.
Under the Texas App Store Accountability Act (SB 2420), app stores are mandated to implement age verification for users, restricting overall access to the NYT app in Texas.

The United Arab Emirates utilizes a sophisticated internet filtering system that periodically blocks certain critical foreign news articles. In 2014, a local publishing partner refused to print an edition of the NYT because it contained a front-page investigation into labor abuses.
Blocked by the Great Firewall in mainland People's Republic of China.

As a US-based company, Patreon blocks access from Islamic Republic of Iran under OFAC regulations and its payment processors do not support transactions with sanctioned countries.

Banned alongside other Russian state media after the annexation of Crimea and blocked at ISP level under sanctions decrees renewed since 2017. OONI recorded anomalies or confirmed blockpages in roughly 85% of Ukrainian measurements of rt.com.

Ofcom revoked RT's broadcast licence in March 2022. Separately, sanctions regulations in force since 29 April 2022 designate TV-Novosti and require internet access providers to take reasonable steps to block rt.com, on penalty of up to GBP 1m. Enforcement is uneven: the blocks are DNS-level, not every provider applies them, and no provider has faced action, so the site is still reachable on many networks.

Major private providers dropped RT America in 2022, forcing it to cease operations. Furthermore, US tech giants have independently banned or restricted RT globally on their platforms. The US government also requires RT to register as a foreign agent under FARA.

Egyptian ISPs blocked Signal in December 2016; Open Whisper Systems initially bypassed this using domain-fronting. While domain-fronting is no longer viable globally after major cloud providers disabled it, the block remains and users in Egypt must now rely on Signal's built-in TLS proxies or VPNs to connect.

Islamic Republic of Iran blocked Signal in January 2021 after millions of users migrated from WhatsApp over privacy-policy concerns. Authorities had labelled encrypted chat apps as criminal content and ordered them removed from local app stores; Signal reported that Iranian censors began dropping all Signal traffic and later added proxy support so users could reconnect.
Roskomnadzor blocked Signal in August 2024, citing anti-terrorism legislation.

Gabon's Ordinance No. 0011/PR/2026 (signed 26 February 2026; published 8 April 2026) sets a digital age of majority of 16 and requires parental consent for under-16 social media access. Platforms must verify users with more than an age or ID check alone — name, address and Personal Identification Number (NIP) — ending online anonymity. Operators have a 12-month transition period, with full compliance expected by February 2027.

Indonesia began deactivating under-16 accounts on designated high-risk platforms from 28 March 2026. The communications ministry named YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, Threads, X, Bigo Live and Roblox among platforms subject to the under-16 restriction.

Islamic Republic of Iran blocked public access to Threads within a day of its July 2023 launch. As a Meta/Instagram-linked service it remains inaccessible under Islamic Republic of Iran's broader blocks on foreign social platforms; VPN use is common among those who still reach it.
Malaysia's under-16 social media ban took effect on 1 June 2026. Platforms must verify users' ages and remove under-16 accounts or face fines of up to RM1 million.

Russia blocked Threads the day after its July 2023 launch. Meta is designated an extremist organisation and its other social products (Facebook, Instagram) have been banned since 2022, so Threads is inaccessible without a VPN.

(Meta had separately shut Threads in Türkiye from April 2024 over data-sharing rulings; service returned on 17 June 2026.)

Phase one covers X, Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok. Platforms have a 12-month transition, with full compliance expected by June 2027.

Viber's messaging and calling service was blocked on mainland Chinese networks during the 2014 crackdown on foreign chat apps; it was reachable only through a VPN in contemporaneous testing.

Egypt does not impose a blanket ban on Viber, but authorities have repeatedly throttled or interfered with VoIP features on messaging apps including Viber and WhatsApp; text messaging generally works. Making international calls over unlicensed VoIP is technically illegal under Article 72 of Egypt's Telecommunication Regulation Law.

Islamic Republic of Iran blocks or filters Viber alongside other major foreign messaging services. The United Kingdom government's 2025 country-information note identifies Viber among the messaging apps blocked in Islamic Republic of Iran.

Oman restricts unlicensed VoIP services: Viber voice and video calls are blocked by local carriers under telecommunications licensing rules, while messaging still works. Human Rights Watch and other groups have long documented Oman's ban on consumer VoIP platforms alongside the United Arab Emirates and Qatar.

Qatar restricts unlicensed VoIP services: Viber voice and video calls are blocked on local networks, while messaging still works. The restriction is part of the same Gulf-region licensing regime that also blocks WhatsApp, Skype, and FaceTime calling.
Roskomnadzor blocked access to Viber in December 2024, citing the app's failure to comply with national legislation and its refusal to remove content regarding the war in Ukraine.
Viber has long been inaccessible in Turkmenistan under the state's broad block on foreign messaging and social-media services.

Viber's calling service remains blocked in the United Arab Emirates under the unlicensed-VoIP regime; Freedom House reports that the block has been in place since 2013. This is a feature restriction rather than a block of text messaging.
Blocked by the government due to concerns over hosted nudity and adult content.

Latvia's National Electronic Mass Media Council (NEPLP) ordered ISPs to block VKontakte, Odnoklassniki and other Russian social networks in May 2022 due to EU sanctions on their owners (Yury Kovalchuk and Vladimir Kiriyenko).
Blocked by the Ukrainian government via ISP bans under Presidential Decree No. 133/2017 targeting Russian tech companies.

India used Section 69A of the Information Technology Act to block WeChat among 59 Chinese apps, citing threats to sovereignty, security and public order. The nationwide app-blocking order remains the controlling restriction in the tracker.
Egypt does not impose a blanket ban on WhatsApp calling, but authorities have repeatedly throttled or interfered with VoIP features; messaging generally works.

Islamic Republic of Iran briefly lifted its WhatsApp ban in December 2024, then cut access again amid the June 2025 conflict with Israel; as of May 2026 authorities say reinstatement is not under consideration.
Jordanian telecom operators restrict WhatsApp VoIP: voice and video calls are frequently blocked on mobile networks while messaging still works.
Qatar restricts unlicensed VoIP services: WhatsApp voice and video calls are blocked on local networks, while messaging still works.

Russia blocked WhatsApp voice and video calls in August 2025, throttled the app nationwide from November, then fully blocked it on 11 February 2026 — pushing its roughly 100 million Russian users towards the state-run Max messenger.

Sudan's Telecommunications and Post Regulatory Authority suspended WhatsApp voice and video calls nationwide from 25 July 2025 as a national-security measure; text messaging and group chats remain available.
WhatsApp voice and video calls are blocked in the United Arab Emirates, where unlicensed VoIP services are prohibited; messaging works normally.

Zoom suspended direct sales and new individual signups in mainland People's Republic of China in August 2020 but still operates in the country through licensed local partners — Bizconf, Suirui Zhumu and Systec Umeet — which handle sales, support and compliance on its behalf.
